lessons.title: The propagation environment
lessons.html:
What is propagation?

Propagation means making new plants. Nurseries and farms propagate plants from seed (vegetables, maize, flowers) or from parts of a plant such as cuttings (herbs, sweet potato, rooibos, many shrubs), division (splitting clumps of plants), or grafting and budding (citrus, avocados, roses, grapevines). You will work under supervision.

Where propagation happens

  • Seedbeds in the open land, for example rooibos seedlings in the Cederberg.
  • Nursery shade houses with shade net to protect young plants from hot sun.
  • Tunnels and greenhouses that keep plants warm and protected from wind and rain.
  • Mist beds where fine water spray keeps cuttings moist while they grow roots.
  • Hardening-off areas where young plants get used to outdoor conditions before planting out.

What young plants need

NeedWhy
WarmthSeeds sprout and cuttings root faster in warm conditions
MoistureYoung plants and cuttings dry out quickly
LightSeedlings need light, but not burning sun
AirGood air movement prevents fungal disease
HygieneClean conditions stop disease, such as damping off, killing seedlings

Your supervisor sets the shade, watering and temperature for each area. Do not change the shade net, open tunnel sides or switch off mist beds unless you are told to. A mist bed left off on a hot afternoon can kill a whole bench of cuttings.

Hygiene in the nursery

  • Wash your hands before work and after the toilet.
  • Clean trays, pots, tools and benches as instructed.
  • Use foot baths at the entrance if the nursery has them.
  • Remove dead and sick plants and put them in the bin, not on the floor.
  • Do not put trays directly on the soil if the rule says to keep them on benches.

lessons.title: Preparing material and media
lessons.html:
Propagation media

The medium is what the plants grow in. It must hold water but also drain well, and be free of disease.

  • Seedling mix: a fine mix, often of composted bark, peat or coir, and vermiculite or perlite.
  • Rooting medium for cuttings: often coarse sand, perlite or bark mixed so it drains well.
  • Potting mix: for plants moved into bags or pots.

Preparing the medium

  1. Use only the mix your supervisor gives you. Do not use garden soil unless told; it can carry disease.
  2. Wet the mix evenly. It should feel damp but not dripping when squeezed.
  3. Fill trays or pots loosely, then tap them to settle the mix. Do not press hard; roots need air.
  4. Level the top.
  5. Wear a dust mask when handling dry mixes or perlite if instructed.

    6. Preparing propagation material

    Seed

    • Check the label: crop, variety, date.
    • Treated seed is coloured. Wear gloves and never eat it.
    • Some seeds need soaking or other treatment first; follow the instructions.

    Cuttings

    • Take cuttings from healthy mother plants, early in the day when plants are full of water.
    • Use sharp, clean secateurs or a knife. Wipe the blade with disinfectant between plants if told.
    • Cut to the length shown, just below a node (the place where a leaf joins the stem).
    • Remove the lower leaves so they do not rot in the medium.
    • Keep cuttings in a cool, wet bag or bucket in the shade.
    • Dip the base in rooting hormone if instructed, wearing gloves.

    Safety

    • Cut away from your body.
    • Wash hands after handling seed, hormones and mixes.
    • Lift bags of mix with bent knees.

lessons.title: Propagating and caring for young plants
lessons.html:
Sowing seed

  1. Make small holes or furrows in the medium at the depth shown. Small seeds go very shallow.
  2. Place one or two seeds per cell, or sow thinly in rows.
  3. Cover lightly with medium or vermiculite.
  4. Water gently with a fine rose so seeds do not wash out.
  5. Label each tray: crop, variety, date sown.

Planting cuttings

  1. Make a hole with a stick so the base is not damaged.
  2. Insert the cutting the right way up to about a third of its length, or as shown.
  3. Firm the medium around it.
  4. Place in the mist bed or shade as instructed and label it.

Routine care after propagation

  • Watering: check every day. Keep the medium moist but not waterlogged. Water early in the day.
  • Checking: look for damping off (seedlings fall over at soil level), mould, insects and slugs. Report problems.
  • Thinning: remove extra seedlings so one strong plant remains per cell.
  • Feeding: give liquid fertiliser only as instructed.
  • Transplanting (pricking out): move seedlings or rooted cuttings to bigger pots when they are ready. Hold them by the leaves, not the stem.
  • Hardening off: move plants step by step to more sun and wind, and water a little less, so they are strong for planting out.
  • Records: write sowing dates, numbers, germination and losses on the label or record sheet.

Cleaning up

Clean benches, trays and tools after work. Put used medium and dead plants in the correct bin. Return tools to the store.

Key points

  • Keep the propagation area clean to stop disease.
  • Use only the mix given; wet it evenly and do not press it hard.
  • Take cuttings from healthy plants and keep them cool and wet.
  • Label every tray with crop, variety and date.
  • Check, water and report problems every day; harden off before planting out.
